subject: ss-pulmonology
title: Neuromuscular and Chest Wall Disorders: Respiratory Assessment and Support

steps.tx: Neuromuscular disease weakens the **diaphragm** and intercostal muscles, so ventilation fails before oxygenation does. The earliest signs are poor sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness from **nocturnal hypoventilation**. Hypercapnia appears late, when the patient is already tiring. Monitoring vital capacity and inspiratory strength lets you act before crisis. Assess respiratory function at every clinic visit in these patients.
steps.say: Neuromuscular disease weakens the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles, so ventilation fails before oxygenation does. The earliest signs are poor sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness, caused by nocturnal hypoventilation. Hypercapnia appears late, when the patient is already tiring. Monitoring vital capacity and inspiratory strength lets you act before a crisis. Assess respiratory function at every clinic visit in these patients.

steps.tx: Three bedside measures guide decisions about ventilatory support. **Forced vital capacity** tends to fall as weakness progresses. **Maximal inspiratory pressure** gauges the strength of the inspiratory muscles. A marked drop in forced vital capacity when lying flat points towards **diaphragm weakness**. Support is considered when forced vital capacity is clearly reduced, particularly during a **myasthenic crisis**.
steps.say: Three bedside measures guide decisions about breathing support. Forced vital capacity tends to fall as weakness progresses. Maximal inspiratory pressure shows how strong the inspiratory muscles are. A marked drop in forced vital capacity when the patient lies flat points towards diaphragm weakness. Support is considered when forced vital capacity is clearly reduced, especially during a myasthenic crisis.

rows: Supine fall in forced vital capacity

steps.tx: **Myasthenic crisis** is acute respiratory failure caused by weakness at the **neuromuscular junction**. Assess bulbar function, **vital capacity** and **maximal inspiratory pressure** without delay. Where these are falling or the patient is tiring, arrange **ventilatory support**, often intubation. Treat the trigger with **intravenous immunoglobulin** or plasma exchange, and stop drugs that impair transmission.

nodes.label: Assess vital capacity and inspiratory pressure

steps.tx: The image links blocked signals at the **neuromuscular junction** to weak breathing muscles and a falling trace of **vital capacity**. When antibodies blunt receptor activation, each breath moves less air and fatigue builds quickly. This visual explains why **myasthenic crisis** counts as respiratory failure and why falling capacity prompts timely **ventilatory support** before exhaustion takes hold.
steps.say: This picture connects poor signal at the junction to weak chest movement and a falling vital capacity trace. As each breath moves less air, fatigue builds and crisis follows. That is why falling capacity prompts timely ventilatory support, with close checks of strength and breathing, before exhaustion takes hold.

vis.caption: Blocked signals weaken breathing and invite timely support Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: In practice, measure FVC and maximal inspiratory pressure regularly in neuromuscular patients. Start **nocturnal noninvasive ventilation** when hypercapnia or nocturnal hypoventilation appears, and manage crisis with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. Use the cough assist when peak cough flow is low. Remember that respiratory failure, not limb weakness, usually causes death in Duchenne patients.
